text: 3 Method

We review the LoRA method in Sec. 3.1 . We develop our context-oriented decomposition in Sec. 3.2 , which provides the basis of our knowledge-preserved adaptation and instruction-previewed adaptation introduced in Sec. 3.3 and Sec. 3.4 , respectively.
3.1 Preliminaries on Low-Rank Adaptation

LoRA suggests that the weight change in LLM finetuning presents a low rank structure, and thus proposes to use the product of two low rank matrices to learn the weight change with the pre-trained weights frozen during finetuning [ 21 ] . Given the pre-trained weight W ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t × d i ​ n W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}} from an LLM, the weight after finetuning can be formulated as:
W ∗ = W + Δ ​ W = W + B ​ A , W^{*}=W+\Delta W=W+{B}{A}, (1)

where W ∗ W^{*} is the weight after finetuning, Δ ​ W \Delta W is the weight change, and B ​ A {B}{A} is the low rank decomposition of Δ ​ W \Delta W into two smaller matrices B ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t × r {B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times r} and A ∈ ℝ r × d i ​ n {A}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_{in}} with an intrinsic rank of r ≪ min ⁡ ( d o ​ u ​ t , d i ​ n ) r\ll\min{(d_{out},d_{in})} . In this way, the number of learnable parameters can be largely reduced by freezing the pre-trained weight W W and only finetuning the matrices B B and A A . LoRA adopts the Kaiming initialization [ 18 ] to randomly initialize A A , and B B is initialized as an all-0 matrix such that Δ ​ W = 0 \Delta W=0 at the start of training to circumvent a deviation from the pre-trained model. After finetuning, the learnable adapter B ​ A BA can be merged into the pre-trained weight W W without changing the original model architecture and introducing extra inference burden.
Despite the success of LoRA-based methods, when building the learnable adapter, existing studies widely ignore the data context from the target ability that users are particularly concerned with.
3.2 Context-Oriented Decomposition

Pre-trained large language models are endowed with multi-faced abilities, such as answering the question regarding world knowledge, common sense reasoning, and instruction following. When different kinds of input messages are fed into an LLM, e.g., a question in some domain and a query to solve a math problem, even though they are processed by the same pre-trained weights, different abilities are triggered. The covariance matrix of each layer’s activation will exhibit different outlier patterns as they are responsive to the task triggered to highlight different aspects of the pre-trained weight. Therefore, the covariance matrix is able to capture task context. Inspired by this insight, we leverage the covariance matrix inside LLM to build adapters catering to a certain ability.

The process of our context-oriented decomposition is shown in Figure 1 . First, we randomly collect some samples from the training data of some task with interest, e.g., question answering or Math, and feed these samples into the LLM used to finetune. Denote X ∈ ℝ d i ​ n × B ​ L X\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times BL} as the input activation of a linear layer where d i ​ n d_{in} is the input dimension, B B is the number of samples we collect, and L L represents the sequence length. We have the covariance matrix C = X ​ X T ∈ ℝ d i ​ n × d i ​ n C=XX^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{in}} . We then perform singular value decomposition for the weight multiplied by the covariance matrix as:
𝚂𝚅𝙳 ⁡ ( W ​ C ) = U ​ Σ ​ V T = ∑ i = 1 R σ i ​ 𝐮 i ​ 𝐯 i T , \verb|SVD|(WC)=U\Sigma V^{T}=\sum_{i=1}^{R}\sigma_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}^{T}, (2)

where W ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t × d i ​ n W\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}} is the weight of this linear layer, U ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t × d o ​ u ​ t U\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{out}} and V ∈ ℝ d i ​ n × d i ​ n V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}\times d_{in}} are orthogonal matrices containing singular vectors 𝐮 i ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t \mathbf{u}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}} and 𝐯 i ∈ ℝ d i ​ n \mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{in}} , Σ ∈ ℝ d o ​ u ​ t × d i ​ n \Sigma\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{out}\times d_{in}} is a diagonal matrix with singular values σ i \sigma_{i} on its diagonal arranged in descending order, and R R is the rank (the number of non-zero singular values) of W ​ C WC , i.e., R ≤ min ⁡ { d o ​ u ​ t , d i ​ n } R\leq\min\{d_{out},d_{in}\} .
To not change the inference result at the initialization of finetuning, we reconstruct W W by:

W ^ = 𝚂𝚅𝙳 ⁡ ( W ​ C ) ​ C − 1 = U ​ Σ ​ ( V T ​ C − 1 ) = ∑ i = 1 R σ i ​ 𝐮 i ​ 𝐯 ^ i T , \hat{W}=\verb|SVD|(WC)C^{-1}=U\Sigma(V^{T}C^{-1})=\sum_{i=1}^{R}\sigma_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{i}^{T}, (3)

where C − 1 C^{-1} denotes the inverse of C C , and 𝐯 ^ i T \hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{T} is the i i -th row vector of V T ​ C − 1 V^{T}C^{-1} . In case the covariance matrix C C is not invertible, we adopt a strategy to dynamically add positive values on the diagonal elements of C C to ensure invertible. Concretely, we multiply a positive coefficient with the average value of the diagonal elements of C C , and add it on the diagonal. Then we calculate the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance between C ​ C − 1 CC^{-1} and an identity matrix. If it is higher than a threshold, we double the coefficient and perform this step again, until the distance reaches below the threshold.

After our context-oriented decomposition, the first several components of 𝐮 i \mathbf{u}_{i} and 𝐯 ^ i \mathbf{\hat{v}}_{i} with the largest singular values σ i \sigma_{i} depict the dominant characteristics of the task associated with C C . We can decide either to maintain these key components to not sacrifice the corresponding ability, or to adapt them for better performance on the task, which leads to our two implementation modes in the following two subsections, respectively.
3.3 Mode 1: Knowledge-Preserved Adaptation

We introduce knowledge-preserved adaptation that enables to learn new tasks while maintaining world knowledge. In this mode, we use the question data from question-answering training data, such as TriviaQA [ 23 ] and Natural Questions [ 27 , 29 ] , to obtain the covariance matrices whose pattern corresponds to the knowledge retrieving ability of the LLM. When finetuning on a new task, as shown in Figure 1 , we use the last r r components with the smallest r r singular values in Eq. ( 3 ) to build learnable adapters as:

( 3 ), Σ [ − r : ] \sqrt{\Sigma}_{[-r:]} is a diagonal matrix with the squared root of the smallest r r singular values on the diagonal, and W ′ W^{\prime} corresponding to the first R − r R-r components in Eq. ( 3 ) is frozen during finetuning. We have W ′ W^{\prime} as the difference between W W and B ​ A BA instead of summing the first R − r R-r components to avoid the numerical error between W ^ \hat{W} and W W introduced by the decomposition and inversion operations. After finetuning, the learned matrices B ∗ B^{*} and A ∗ A^{*} can be merged into W ′ W^{\prime} as W ∗ = W ′ + B ∗ ​ A ∗ W^{*}=W^{\prime}+B^{*}A^{*} . This mode is featured by preserving world knowledge as the knowledge retrieving ability captured by the principle R − r R-r components is frozen. It is also more effective than a zero-initialized adapter in learning new abilities as verified by our experiments.
3.4 Mode 2: Instruction-Previewed Adaptation

In the circumstance that pursuing a higher performance on the finetuning task is the priority, our instruction-previewed adaptation will be favorable. In this mode, we collect instruction and response from the training data used for finetuning, e.g. the query to solve a math problem and its answer shown in Figure 1 as an example. The prompts are fed into the LLM to produce the covariance matrices whose pattern is associated with the task to learn. We use the first r r components with the largest r r singular values in Eq. ( 3 ) to build learnable adapters as:
W ′ = W − B A , B = U [ : , : r ] Σ [ : r ] , A = Σ [ : r ] ( V T C − 1 ) [ : r , : ] , W^{\prime}=W-BA,\quad B=U_{[:,:r]}\sqrt{\Sigma}_{[:r]},\quad A=\sqrt{\Sigma}_{[:r]}(V^{T}C^{-1})_{[:r,:]}, (5)

where B B and A A are the initialized matrices in the learnable adapter, B ​ A = ∑ i = 1 r σ i ​ 𝐮 i ​ 𝐯 ^ i T BA=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{\hat{v}}_{i}^{T} corresponds to the first r r components in Eq. ( 3 ), Σ [ : r ] \sqrt{\Sigma}_{[:r]} is the squared root of the largest r r singular values in a diagonal matrix. Similar to knowledge-preserved adaptation, W ′ W^{\prime} containing the remaining R − r R-r components is frozen during finetuning. This mode enables the initialized adapters to pre-capture the main characteristics of the finetuning task, leading to stronger performance after training. A recently proposed method [ 43 ] also performs SVD and uses the first r r components to initialize an adapter for finetuning. However, their decomposition is agnostic with respect to any data context. Our adapter capturing the task context in advance can well accommodate the new ability and lead to better finetuning performances in our experiments.
